name: Elena Patel

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me, Elena. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I buy for Brightway Supplies, which sells paper, pens, art kits and classroom furniture to schools and offices. Mornings I check the stock report and chase two or three suppliers, and after lunch I sit with Rhona, our purchasing manager, going over quotes. August is chaos because every school wants everything the same week. I'm still the junior, three years in after working the customer desk, so a lot of my day is learning how not to over-order glitter.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: And outside of work, who's at home with you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My husband Sanjay is an electrician, he works for a firm doing school and clinic wiring, and we have Asha, ten, and Dev, seven. We bought a semi on Northgate Road four years ago, the mortgage is big but we've kept a solid cushion, maybe nine months of bills. I do the school run on Tuesdays and Thursdays, Sanjay does the rest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fine, let's see it prove itself. At work I'd say it's useful for drafting a supplier email and not much else yet. To my friends I'd say don't believe the hype or the doom, wait for the numbers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly I don't lose sleep. Schools will always buy paper, pens and chairs, Sanjay's work is steady, and we've got savings. The only bit that nags is that routine reorders are what the software would take, and I do a lot of those.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing the job and use the AI a bit more, maybe for first drafts of price comparisons. I'd ask Rhona to let me run a few of the supplier negotiations so I'm not just on reorders. We'd carry on with the mortgage overpayment, 150 a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty calm. A normal level of busy and a normal level of money worry. I'd say it feels like another Tuesday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you use AI now and then. What for, exactly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I put a supplier's price list into the chatbot last month and asked it to compare three quotes, and it got one number wrong, which I only saw because I'd checked. So I use it like a keen intern. That's why I'm not scared of the plateau world, I know its limits.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does any of this change how you see Rhona and the team?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rhona would stay, she's got twenty years of supplier relationships. The part-timers on reorders might get fewer hours, and that makes me wince. If I was asked, I'd say don't trim the people who know the customers.

say: I'd say let's see it **prove** itself, since it drafts a supplier email nicely and not much else yet.
To friends I'd say don't believe the hype or the **doom**, wait for the numbers.
think: I don't lose sleep, because schools will always buy paper and Sanjay's wiring work is **steady**.
The one nag is that routine reorders are what software would take, and I do many.
do: Use the AI a little more for first drafts of **price** comparisons.
Ask Rhona to let me run a few supplier **negotiations**.
Keep overpaying the mortgage by **150** a month.
feel: Pretty **calm**, a normal level of busy and a normal level of money worry.
S0.quote: I use it like a keen intern. That's why I'm not scared of the plateau world, I know its limits.
fieldNote: Practical and evidence-minded, which keeps her steady when little changes.
Sees her routine reorders as the one soft spot even in a quiet world.
Worries more for the **part-timers** than for herself.

steps.text: Use the AI chatbot for first drafts of price comparisons
Ask Rhona for supplier negotiations beyond routine reorders
Overpay the mortgage by 150 a month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say something like, it's a real change and we should treat people fairly while it happens. At work I'd ask for a plan: which tasks go to software, which stay with us, and what happens to the hours. Online I'd probably share articles about retraining and ask my union rep, we do have a small branch, to put it on the agenda.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I think the buying side shrinks. Quotes, comparisons, reorder forecasts, the software will do those quicker than me. I'm three years in and still learning, so I'm probably first in the queue, and I'd be daft to pretend otherwise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sign up for the evening course on supply-chain planning the college runs, and I'd offer to be the person who tests the new tools for Rhona. I'd keep two months of extra savings on top of what we have, and Sanjay and I would sit down and look at what we'd cut if my wage dropped. I'd also keep my CV fresh, because plenty of distributors nearby are hiring for customer-facing roles.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tense but able to cope. I feel I have some control because I can learn the tools and there's cash behind us. I'm worried, and I'd say so if you asked me straight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Rhona if she asked you to train the team on the new tools?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say yes, happily, but I'd want the training in work hours, not my evenings. And I'd say be honest with the team about which roles are likely to shrink. People can handle a hard truth better than a vague one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which tasks would you hold on to for as long as possible?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Negotiating, because it's about knowing the people and the history behind the price. Checking deliveries when something goes wrong, because suppliers lie by accident all the time and you need a human who will ring up and be cross. The data entry and the forecast I can see going to software.

say: I'd say it's a real change and we should treat people **fairly**, with a plan for which tasks go to software.
I'd ask our small union branch to put it on the **agenda**.
think: The buying side shrinks, since quotes and forecasts are what software does **quicker** than me.
Three years in and still learning, I'm probably **first** in the queue.
do: Sign up for the college evening course on supply-chain **planning**.
Offer to be the person who **tests** new tools for Rhona.
Save two months more and review what we'd **cut** if my wage dropped.
feel: **Tense** but able to cope, because I can learn the tools and there's cash behind us.
S1.quote: People can handle a hard truth better than a vague one.
fieldNote: She expects her own role to shrink but feels she has some control.
Uses AI a little already, so her plan is to be the **tester**, not the victim.
Wants honesty from management and training in paid hours.

steps.text: Enrol in the college evening course on supply-chain planning
Offer to test the new buying tools for Rhona
Save two months of extra cushion
Ask the union branch to put the plan on the agenda

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need rules in place before it's here, such as notice periods and retraining funds paid for by the firms that save money. At work I'd say let's get ahead and decide what we want from the tools. To friends I'd say vote for people who have a plan, not people who say it won't happen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My job at my desk is gone around 2028, I'm fairly sure of that. Sanjay's wiring gets about three more years, because robots that can crawl through a school ceiling are further away. So we're a household where my work goes first and his goes later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd try to become the person at Brightway who manages the AI buyer, I'd learn it properly in the first year. If it doesn't work out I'd move over to the customer account side, which is people-facing. I'd put the extra savings into a joint account, cancel the family trip to the coast, and ask the bank about a payment holiday in advance, not after.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared but not frozen. It's about two years of fast change and not enough time to be sure of anything. The cushion helps, I won't pretend it doesn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How do you picture the first six months after AGI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First six months, I think firms freeze hiring, then the first round of layoffs in the buying and admin teams. I'd expect Rhona to be kept because she holds relationships. I'd be on the fence, so I'd try to be useful in a way they can see.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Sanjay about the electrician work, given robots come later?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got three years of breathing space on his side, so let's use it, you keep taking the big contracts, and I'll move into something people-facing. I'd also tell him not to rely on the three years, since the planning and quoting part of his job will go sooner.

say: I'd say we need **rules** before it's here, like notice periods and retraining funds paid for by the firms that save money.
To friends I'd say vote for people with a **plan**.
think: My desk job is **gone** around 2028, while Sanjay's wiring gets about three more years.
In our household my work goes first and his goes **later**.
do: Learn the AI buyer properly and try to be the person who **manages** it.
Move to the **customer** account side if that doesn't work.
Ask the bank about a payment **holiday** in advance.
feel: **Scared** but not frozen, with about two years of fast change and not enough time to be sure.
S2.quote: My job at my desk is gone around 2028, I'm fairly sure of that.
fieldNote: Reads the card closely: her thinking work goes first and her husband's hands-on work about three years later.
Expects to lose her job or a large part of her income on the stated date.
Shows a steady person's plan: manage the tool, or move to **people-facing** work.

steps.text: Learn the AI buying system well enough to supervise it
Move to the customer account side if buying shrinks
Ask the bank about a payment holiday in advance
Cancel the coast holiday and save the money

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to do this properly, if people start now. At work I'd push for a joint training plan, and to the union branch I'd say it's time to bargain for retraining time. I'd tell my friends to learn the tools while they're cheap and easy to try.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's better but I still don't think my buying job lasts to 2031. The extra three years mean I can finish a course and shift into planning or customer work before the chop. I'd say the cushion feels bigger when the clock is slower.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd finish the supply-chain planning course and start looking at roles in the distribution centre planning team. I'd also save three hundred a month, up from one-fifty. Sanjay and I would talk about whether he wants to train as a solar installer, since that's hands-on and growing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Better than the two-year version, I'd say anxious but hopeful. I'd feel I could steer a little.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Five years versus two. What do you do with the extra time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the time to try one new role every year. Planning first, then maybe customer success. I'd also hold off on any big spending like the kitchen, and I'd rather sit on the cash.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Asha and Dev, in simple words?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, mummy's job is to work with computers, and computers are about to get a lot cleverer, so mummy is learning new things so we're ready. I'd tell them it's good to be curious and good to be kind, and that people who can fix things and talk to people will always be needed.

say: I'd say five years is enough to do it **properly** if people start now, with a joint training plan at work.
I'd tell friends to learn the tools while they're **cheap** to try.
think: I still don't think my buying job lasts to **2031**, but I could shift into planning first.
The cushion feels **bigger** when the clock runs slower.
do: Finish the supply-chain planning **course** and look at planning roles in the distribution centre.
Talk with Sanjay about training as a **solar** installer.
feel: **Anxious** but hopeful, feeling I can steer a little.
S3.quote: I'd say, mummy's job is to work with computers, and computers are about to get a lot cleverer, so mummy is learning new things so we're ready.
fieldNote: The extra years turn her worry into a sequence of small career moves.
Brings her **husband's** options into the plan, showing a household view.
Hopeful tone, but still expects the buying job to go.

steps.text: Apply for planning roles in the distribution centre
Ask Sanjay to look at solar installer training

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a decent runway, and the question is who pays for the transition. At work I'd say let's build skills slowly and not panic. I'd ask friends to vote for retraining funds and a fair tax on the companies that profit most.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In ten years I'm fifty-three, Asha is twenty and Dev is seventeen. I think my desk job is gone by then, but I'd have had a decade to move into something else. I'd honestly feel okay, not great, but okay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing the job well, learn AI tools a bit each year, and take a course every year or two instead of cramming. I'd pay the mortgage off faster, aiming to clear it by the time the kids are at university. I'd probably also move to a planning role in the next few years, while it's calm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fairly relaxed. The big worry would be whether anyone actually builds the retraining systems everyone promises. If they don't, ten years vanishes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years feels like a lot. Does it change your attitude at work now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd look at it differently, less scared. I'd treat AI as the thing my career runs alongside, not something that ends it. I'd still use it just now and then, but I'd get better at it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want from government or from your employer in that time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: From the employer, paid time to retrain and honesty about where roles are going. From government, a proper fund and training that isn't a leaflet. I'd say I'd happily pay a bit more tax if it's actually spent on that.

say: I'd say ten years is a decent runway, and the real question is who **pays** for the transition.
I'd ask friends to vote for **retraining** funds.
think: By ten years my desk job is probably gone, but I'd have had a **decade** to move on.
I'd feel okay, not great, as long as the **systems** really get built.
do: Learn AI tools **a bit** each year and take a course every year or two.
Aim to clear the **mortgage** by the time the kids are at university.
Move to a **planning** role in the next few years while it's calm.
feel: Fairly **relaxed**, with one worry about whether anyone really builds the retraining.
S4.quote: I'd treat AI as the thing my career runs alongside, not something that ends it.
fieldNote: With a decade, she settles on slow, paced change rather than a rush.
Her concern is **who pays**, which matches her left-leaning views.
Steady adaptability shows: use the tool just now and then, but get better.

steps.text: Take one work-related course every year or two
Learn a new AI tool each year
Move into a planning role in the next few years
Pay off the mortgage before the kids reach university

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because there isn't enough time for companies or families to prepare. What would help is paid retraining time from my employer, a real government fund, and honest talk about which roles are going. The savings and Sanjay's steady job help too, but I wouldn't want to lean on them.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: I'd just say that I'm not against AI, I'm against it landing on people with no plan. I use it a bit already and it's handy. Done fairly, it could be good for the kids.

headlineQuote: I'm not against AI, I'm against it landing on people with no plan.
portrait: Elena is a **43-year-old** junior buyer at Brightway Supplies, selling paper, art kits and classroom furniture to schools and offices.
She uses AI **now and then**, like a keen intern, and trusts what she can check herself.
The household has a big mortgage, two children and about nine months of savings, with Sanjay's steady electrician work.
She expects her **buying** job to go in the AGI worlds, and plans to learn, retrain or move to people-facing work.
She leans on **fairness**: paid retraining, honest bosses and a fair tax on the firms that profit.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** picture worries her most because families and firms have no time to prepare.
whatWouldHelp: Paid **retraining** time from her employer, a real government fund and honest talk about which roles go.
